title: Gathering the hymns
hook: with Bhai Gurdas as scribe, he gathers the Gurus' hymns and those of other saints into one book

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Harmandir Sahib: built low, with a door on every side. Your line was open on every side. Did you leave a door open for someone? Day sixty-one.

Think about the songs your family actually sings. A grandmother's lullaby. The hymn at every funeral. The tune someone hums in the kitchen. Most of them were never written down. They live in people, and when the people go, verses slip away, words drift, and sometimes someone adds a verse of their own and passes it off as the old one. By the time of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, the Sikh community had four Gurus' worth of hymns, sung every day, copied in handwritten books kept by different families. And other people were starting to write hymns in Guru Nanak's name that he never wrote. Guru Arjan decided the words needed one home. Today, the gathering.
screen: `SONGS THAT LIVE IN PEOPLE.` → `FOUR GURUS' WORTH OF HYMNS.` → `ONE HOME FOR THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Around 1603, at a quiet spot by a pool near Amritsar, Guru Arjan sat down to make a book. His scribe was Bhai Gurdas, a scholar and poet who was also the Guru's relative, and whose own verses Sikhs still read. The Guru dictated; Bhai Gurdas wrote. First, the Guru gathered. Earlier Gurus' hymns had been collected in handwritten volumes under the third Guru, and tradition says those books were kept by his son, Baba Mohan, who would not hand them over. So Guru Arjan went to his house and sang outside his window, a hymn in his honor, until Mohan came down and gave them up. Second, the Guru sorted. He set the hymns not by author or by date, but by raga, the musical mode each one was meant to be sung in, so the book is laid out like a songbook for the day and its moods. Third, and this is the surprise, he opened the book to others. Beside the Gurus' words he placed hymns by saints from outside the Sikh community: Kabir, a weaver from Benares; Namdev, a calico printer; Ravidas, a leatherworker whom his society called untouchable; and Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi who had lived centuries before. Hindu and Muslim, high caste and low, sitting on the same pages, because the Guru found in them the same truth about the one God. And he left some things out: the hymns written falsely in Nanak's name did not go in. Gather, sort, open the pages, and guard them. That is how a scattered songbook became one book.
screen: `GURU ARJAN DICTATES, BHAI GURDAS WRITES.` · `SINGING FOR THE OLD BOOKS.` · `SORTED BY RAGA, LIKE A SONGBOOK.` · `KABIR, RAVIDAS, FARID ON ONE PAGE.` · then, large: `ONE HOME FOR THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather one thing worth keeping. Settle and breathe for a moment. Then let your mind go looking, the way the Guru went looking. A line someone said to you that you've never forgotten. A recipe only one person in your family knows. A song, a joke, a piece of advice. Pick one. Now picture where it lives right now: in one person's head, on a scrap of paper, in a phone that could break. Just hold it for a while, and ask where it would be safe. The bell holds the time.
Gathering the hymns. Guru Arjan, with Bhai Gurdas writing, collected the Gurus' hymns and those of other saints, sorted them by raga, and made them one book.
Your line: gather what is true. Today, write down the thing you chose, or ask the person who holds it to tell you again, and keep it somewhere safe. Day sixty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Arjan as the compiler of the Adi Granth, the book that became the Guru Granth Sahib, and the hymns of Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, Farid and other saints are sung in gurdwaras alongside the Gurus' own.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a raga, the musical mode that orders the hymns of the book.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone copied some hymns into a book.
what it means: Guru Arjan gathered, sorted and guarded the Gurus' words, and opened the pages to saints of other communities.
what a scholar hears: the Adi Granth drew on earlier collections from Guru Amar Das's time, and set every hymn under its raga rather than its author.

notes: Date and place: compilation traditionally at Ramsar, Amritsar, c. 1603–1604. Confirm 'around 1603'.
Bhai Gurdas described as the Guru's relative (traditionally his maternal uncle's son / uncle of Guru Arjan's mother's line); stated only as 'relative'. Confirm.
Baba Mohan (son of Guru Amar Das) and the Goindval pothis; the window-singing episode (hymn 'Mohan tere oohe mandar', Ang 248) is tradition. Confirm framing.
Occupations given for the bhagats (Kabir weaver, Namdev calico printer/tailor, Ravidas leatherworker) are traditional; confirm wording, especially 'whom his society called untouchable'.
The exclusion of spurious compositions in Nanak's name (associated with Prithi Chand's line, the Minas) is stated generally; the jealous brother is day 59. Confirm.
